passages.quote: A valve is a mechanical device that controls the flow of fluid and pressure within a system or process.
Regardless of type, all valves have the following basic parts: the body, bonnet, trim (internal elements), actuator, and packing.
The body, sometimes called the shell, is the primary pressure boundary of a valve.
The cover for the opening in the valve body is the bonnet.
The internal elements of a valve are collectively referred to as a valve's trim
The disk provides the capability for permitting and prohibiting fluid flow.
The seat or seal rings provide the seating surface for the disk.
connects the actuator and disk, is responsible for positioning the disk.
The actuator operates the stem and disk assembly.
Most valves use some form of packing to prevent leakage from the space between the stem and the bonnet.
If a valve's packing is too loose, the valve will leak, which is a safety hazard. If the packing is too tight, it will impair the movement and possibly damage the stem.
In general, there are four methods of controlling flow through a valve.
For a rising stem valve, the stem will rise above the actuator as the valve is opened.
A gate valve is a linear motion valve used to start or stop fluid flow; however, it does not regulate or throttle flow.
Hence, there is little pressure drop across an open gate valve.
Most of the flow change occurs near shutoff with a relatively high fluid velocity causing disk and seat wear and eventual leakage if used to regulate flow.
A globe valve is a linear motion valve used to stop, start, and regulate fluid flow.
When compared to a gate valve, a globe valve generally yields much less seat leakage.
The most evident shortcoming of the simple globe valve is the high head loss from two or more right angle turns of flowing fluid.
The backseat design prevents system pressure from building against the valve packing.
A ball valve is a rotational motion valve that uses a ball-shaped disk to stop or start fluid flow.
A ball valve is generally the least expensive of any valve configuration and has low maintenance costs.
Conventional ball valves have relatively poor throttling characteristics.
A plug valve is a rotational motion valve used to stop or start fluid flow.
Multiport valves are particularly advantageous on transfer lines and for diverting services.
A diaphragm valve is a linear motion valve that is used to start, regulate, and stop fluid flow.
Diaphragm valves are particularly suited for the handling of corrosive fluids, fibrous slurries, radioactive fluids, or other fluids that must remain free from contamination.
Reducing valves automatically reduce supply pressure to a preselected pressure as long as the supply pressure is at least as high as the selected pressure.
Pinch valves are suitable for on-off and throttling services.
A butterfly valve, illustrated in Figure 19, is a rotary motion valve that is used to stop, regulate, and start fluid flow.

Butterfly valves are especially well-suited for the handling of large flows of liquids or gases at relatively low pressures and for the handling of slurries or liquids with large amounts of suspended solids.
A needle valve, as shown in Figure 20, is used to make relatively fine adjustments in the amount of fluid flow.
Check valves are designed to prevent the reversal of flow in a piping system.
Swing check valves are usually installed in conjunction with gate valves because they provide relatively free flow.
A lift check valve, illustrated in Figure 24, is commonly used in piping systems in which globe valves are being used as a flow control valve.
A stop check valve, illustrated in Figure 27, is a combination of a lift check valve and a globe valve.
The main difference between a relief valve and a safety valve is the extent of opening at the setpoint pressure.
The difference between the actuating pressure setpoint and the pressure at which the safety valve resets is called blowdown.
Relief valves are typically used for incompressible fluids such as water or oil.
Safety valves can often be distinguished by the presence of an external lever at the top of the valve body, which is used as an operational check.
Manual actuators are capable of placing the valve in any position but do not permit automatic operation.
All actuators except manual handwheel and lever are adaptable to automatic actuation.
With this arrangement, the valve can be pounded shut for tight closure or pounded open if it is stuck shut.
The motor is usually a, reversible, high speed type connected through a gear train to reduce the motor speed and thereby increase the torque at the stem.
Limit switches are normally provided to stop the motor automatically at full open and full closed valve positions.
These actuators translate an air signal into valve stem motion by air pressure acting on a diaphragm or piston connected to the stem.
These actuators use a piston to convert a signal pressure into valve stem motion.
Solenoids position the valve by attracting a magnetic slug attached to the valve stem.
Double solenoid valves typically fail "as is."
In general, fastest actuation is provided by hydraulic, pneumatic, and solenoid actuators.
However, solenoids are not practical for large valves because their size and power requirements would be excessive.
Upon a loss of power, an MOV will fail as is.

items: Varying (throttling) the amount of fluid flow
Controlling the direction of fluid flow
Regulating downstream system or process pressure
Relieving component or piping over pressure
Move a disc or plug into or against an orifice, as in a globe or needle valve
Slide a flat, cylindrical, or spherical surface across an orifice, as in gate and plug valves
Rotate a disc or ellipse about a shaft across the diameter of an orifice, as in a butterfly or ball valve
Move a flexible material into the flow passage, as in diaphragm and pinch valves

checks.q: Which is one of the four basic methods of controlling flow through a valve?
o: Reverse the direction of the pump
Heat the fluid to change its density
Add a second fluid to the line
Move a flexible material into the flow passage
checks.x: The four methods are moving a disc or plug against an orifice, sliding a surface across an orifice, rotating a disc or ellipse about a shaft, and moving a flexible material into the flow passage.

checks.q: Which flow control method does a butterfly valve use?
o: Sliding a flat surface across the orifice
Moving a plug into the orifice
Moving a flexible material into the passage
Rotating a disc about a shaft across the orifice
checks.x: Rotating a disc or ellipse about a shaft extending across the diameter of an orifice applies to a butterfly or ball valve.

body.alt: Valve cross section labeling the actuator, packing, bonnet, stem, body, disk, and seat.

body.text: The body resists fluid pressure loads from connecting piping and receives the piping through threaded, bolted, or welded joints.
The bonnet is the second principal pressure boundary, and it is a potential source of leakage.
The trim typically includes a disk, seat, stem, and sleeves that guide the stem.
The stem connects the actuator and disk.

body.alt: Rising stem gate valve, closed and open, with the stem extending above the handwheel when open.

body.text: A nonrising stem shows no upward movement outside the valve. The disk is threaded internally and travels on the stem.

body.alt: Nonrising stem gate valve, closed and open, with the gate traveling on the stem threads.

checks.q: Which part is the primary pressure boundary of a valve?
checks.x: The body, sometimes called the shell, is the primary pressure boundary of a valve.

checks.q: What is the purpose of the valve stem?
o: It is the first pressure boundary
It connects the actuator and disk and positions the disk
It seals the bonnet to the body
checks.x: The stem connects the actuator and disk and is responsible for positioning the disk.

checks.q: How is valve stem leakage controlled?
o: By properly compressing the packing around the stem
checks.x: Valve packing must be properly compressed to prevent fluid loss and damage to the stem.

checks.q: What happens if valve packing is too tight?
o: The disk falls off the stem
It impairs valve movement and may damage the stem
checks.x: If the packing is too tight, it will impair the movement and possibly damage the stem.

body.alt: Cutaway gate valve labeling the handwheel, stem, packing, bonnet, gate, and body.

body.text: The disk is completely out of the flow stream when the valve is fully open, so it offers virtually no resistance to flow.
Flow does not change evenly with stem travel, and a partly open gate disk tends to vibrate. For these reasons gate valves are not used to throttle.

body.alt: Z-body globe valve labeling the handwheel, stem, bonnet, disk, and seat, with flow turning through the body.

body.text: The disk moves perpendicular to the seat, so the annular space closes gradually. This gives the globe valve good throttling ability.

checks.q: Why are gate valves not used to throttle flow?
o: Most flow change occurs near shutoff, and high velocity wears the disk and seat
They have too much head loss when open
checks.x: Most of the flow change occurs near shutoff with a relatively high fluid velocity causing disk and seat wear and eventual leakage if used to regulate flow.

checks.q: What is the main drawback of a simple globe valve?
o: High head loss from two or more right angle turns
checks.x: The most evident shortcoming of the simple globe valve is the high head loss from two or more right angle turns of flowing fluid.

checks.q: What does a globe valve backseat do?
o: Limits flow when the valve is open
Prevents system pressure from building against the packing
Seals the disk when the valve is closed
checks.x: The backseat design prevents system pressure from building against the valve packing.

body.alt: Ball valve cross section with a ball that has a hole through it, between two seats.

body.text: Most ball valves need a 90° turn of the handle. When the handle lies along the axis of the valve, the valve is open.
Ball valves also offer quick, quarter turn on-off operation, are compact, require no lubrication, and give tight sealing with low torque.
In a throttling position the partly exposed seat erodes rapidly from high velocity flow. Elastomeric seats also keep these valves from elevated temperatures.

body.alt: Plug valve with a solid plug bored through at right angles to its axis.

body.text: The passage in the plug lines up with the valve ports when open, and a 90° turn blocks them.
One multiport valve can replace three or four shutoff valves, but many configurations do not completely shut off flow.

checks.q: What is a common use of a multiport plug valve?
checks.x: Multiport valves are particularly advantageous on transfer lines and for diverting services.

checks.q: In a ball valve, what shows that the valve is open?
o: The stem rises above the handwheel
The handle lies across the axis of the valve
The handle lies along the axis of the valve
checks.x: When the handle lies along the axis of the valve, the valve is open. When it lies 90° across the axis, the valve is closed.

concepts.title: Diaphragm, pinch, butterfly, needle, and reducing valves

body.alt: Straight through diaphragm valve in three positions, with a flexible diaphragm pressed against the body.
Weir diaphragm valve in cross section, with the compressor pressing the diaphragm onto a raised weir.

body.text: The operating mechanism is not exposed to the fluid, and there are no packing glands to maintain.

body.alt: Pinch valve with a rubber sleeve squeezed by an external pinching device.

body.text: Pinch valves suit slurries and liquids with large amounts of suspended solids, because the operating mechanism is completely isolated from the fluid.

body.alt: Butterfly valve with a disk on a stem inside a short body.

body.text: A 90° rotation of the handle moves the disk from fully closed to fully open. Savings in weight, space, and cost are the most obvious advantages, especially for large valves.

body.alt: Needle valve with a long, tapered point on the end of the stem entering the seat.

body.text: The long, tapered point acts as a disk and passes through the orifice before it seats, so the opening changes very gradually.

body.alt: Variable reducing valve showing the main valve, piston, auxiliary valve, controlling diaphragm, and adjusting spring and screw.

body.text: An adjusting spring pushes against a diaphragm, and reduced outlet pressure opposes it. The balance positions the auxiliary valve, and so the main valve.

checks.q: Which valve suits fluids that must stay free of contamination, such as radioactive fluids?
checks.x: Diaphragm valves are particularly suited for corrosive fluids, fibrous slurries, radioactive fluids, or other fluids that must remain free from contamination.

checks.q: Which valve is especially suited to large flows at relatively low pressures?
checks.x: Butterfly valves are especially well-suited for the handling of large flows of liquids or gases at relatively low pressures.

checks.q: Which valve is used for relatively fine adjustments of flow?
checks.x: A needle valve is used to make relatively fine adjustments in the amount of fluid flow.

checks.q: What does a reducing valve do?
o: Automatically reduces supply pressure to a preselected pressure
Isolates a system with no leakage
checks.x: Reducing valves automatically reduce supply pressure to a preselected pressure as long as the supply pressure is at least as high as the selected pressure.

checks.q: A valve is a rubber sleeve squeezed by an external mechanism. What type is it?
checks.x: The pinch control valve consists of a sleeve molded of rubber or other synthetic material and a pinching mechanism.

body.text: Flow opens the valve, and any reversal of flow closes it. Closure comes from the weight of the check mechanism, back pressure, a spring, or a combination.

body.alt: Swing check valve with a disk hinged at the top.

body.text: A swing check gives full, unobstructed flow, and turbulence and pressure drop are very low.
Swing checks suit low velocity flow. Pulsating flow would make the disk flap and destroy the seating elements.

body.alt: Lift check valve with a guided disk that lifts off its seat as flow enters below.

body.text: Flow to a lift check must always enter below the seat. Backflow and gravity force the disk or ball onto the seat.

body.alt: Stop check valve with a stem that can hold the disk on its seat, on a globe type body.

body.text: With the stem closed, the disk cannot leave the seat, as in a globe valve. With the stem open, the valve works as a lift check. The stem is not connected to the disk.

checks.q: What is the purpose of a check valve?
o: To prevent the reversal of flow in a piping system
checks.x: Check valves are designed to prevent the reversal of flow in a piping system.

checks.q: Why should swing check valves be kept off lines with pulsating flow?
o: They cannot open against pulsing flow
Their pressure drop is too high
They block flow in both directions
The continual flapping would destroy the seating elements
checks.x: They should not be used on lines with pulsating flow when the continual flapping or pounding would be destructive to the seating elements.

checks.q: What combination makes up a stop check valve?
o: A swing check valve and a gate valve
A safety valve and a relief valve
A butterfly valve and a ball valve
A lift check valve and a globe valve
checks.x: A stop check valve is a combination of a lift check valve and a globe valve.

body.text: Relief and safety valves prevent equipment damage by relieving accidental over-pressurization of fluid systems.

body.alt: Relief valve with a spring holding the disk on the seat and a side outlet.

body.text: A relief valve gradually opens as inlet pressure rises above the setpoint, and only as far as needed.

body.alt: Safety valve with a spring, adjusting nuts on the yoke, and an external lever at the top.

body.text: A safety valve rapidly pops fully open at the pressure setting and stays open until pressure drops below a reset pressure.
Blowdown is expressed as a percentage of the actuating pressure setpoint.
Safety valves are typically used for compressible fluids such as steam or other gases.
Most of these valves open against a compression spring, and the adjusting nuts set the pressure.

checks.q: How can a safety valve often be told apart from a relief valve?
o: A flow arrow on the bonnet
An external lever at the top of the valve body
checks.x: Safety valves can often be distinguished by the presence of an external lever at the top of the valve body, which is used as an operational check.

checks.q: What is the main difference between a relief valve and a safety valve?
o: The extent of opening at the setpoint pressure
checks.x: The main difference between a relief valve and a safety valve is the extent of opening at the setpoint pressure.

body.alt: Handwheel fixed directly to a valve stem.

body.text: A handwheel fixed to the stem gives only the mechanical advantage of the wheel.

body.alt: Hammer handwheel with a primary wheel, a secondary wheel, and lugs.

body.text: A hammer handwheel moves freely through part of its turn and then hits a lug on a secondary wheel attached to the stem.

body.alt: Manual gear head with a pinion and valve gear on the bonnet.

body.text: Gear heads add mechanical advantage, so one person can operate the valve, but operating time for large valves is exceptionally long.

checks.q: What do manual actuators not permit?
o: Placing the valve in an intermediate position
checks.x: Manual actuators are capable of placing the valve in any position but do not permit automatic operation.

checks.q: What is a hammer handwheel for?
o: Pounding a valve shut for tight closure, or open if stuck
checks.x: With this arrangement, the valve can be pounded shut for tight closure or pounded open if it is stuck shut.

body.alt: Electric motor actuator: a motor drives a gear train with limit switches, and a handwheel engages the same gears.

body.text: Direction of motor rotation sets direction of disk motion, and a handwheel can be engaged for manual operation.

body.alt: Pneumatic actuator with air pressure acting on a diaphragm above a spring, connected through the stem to the valve.

body.text: When air pressure closes the valve and spring action opens it, the actuator is direct-acting. When air pressure opens it and spring action closes it, the actuator is reverse-acting. Duplex actuators have air on both sides of the diaphragm.
Hydraulic fluid is fed to one side of the piston while the other side is drained or bled. Solenoid valves typically direct the fluid.

body.alt: Solenoid actuated valve with a coil around a magnetic slug on the stem, a spring, and a manual override.

body.text: In a single solenoid valve, a spring acts against the slug, and removing power returns the valve to the opposite position. Fail open valves are opened by the spring and closed by energizing the solenoid. Fail closed valves are the reverse.

checks.q: What stops an electric motor actuator at full open and full closed?
o: An orifice in the air line
checks.x: Limit switches are normally provided to stop the motor automatically at full open and full closed valve positions.

checks.q: A pneumatic actuator closes the valve with air pressure and opens it with a spring. What is it called?
checks.x: When air pressure closes the valve and spring action opens the valve, the actuator is termed direct-acting.

checks.q: How does a solenoid position a valve?
o: By pressing air on a diaphragm
By feeding hydraulic fluid to a piston
By attracting a magnetic slug attached to the stem
checks.x: Solenoids position the valve by attracting a magnetic slug attached to the valve stem.

checks.q: Why are solenoids not used on large valves?
o: Their size and power requirements would be excessive
checks.x: Solenoids are not practical for large valves because their size and power requirements would be excessive.

concepts.title: Valve position and good operating practice

body.text: Remote position indication uses lights driven by a detector that senses stem, disk, or actuator position, such as a mechanical limit switch or a magnetic switch.
body.cite: Word: Valve Fundamentals.docx, slide 1.70 Valve Position Indication

body.text: Locally, a rising stem shows position, and nonrising stem and power actuated valves often use mechanical pointers.
body.cite: Word: Valve Fundamentals.docx, slide 1.70 Valve Position Indication

body.text: Opening a valve slowly also lets the system stabilize as flow rates change. Use both hands where the design allows, and do not use unapproved aids such as cheater bars.
body.cite: Word: Valve Fundamentals.docx, slide 1.54 Manual Valve Operation

body.text: Parts of different materials and thicknesses cool at different rates. Yoke arms contract faster than the body and compress the stem, which causes the valve to bind.
body.cite: Word: Valve Fundamentals.docx, slide 1.57 Thermal Binding of Gate Valves

body.text: Closing a valve results in decreased flow and increased backpressure upstream of the valve.
body.cite: Word: Valve Fundamentals.docx, slide 1.63 Valve Position and Fluid Flow

checks.q: Why should valves always be opened slowly?
o: To reduce the setpoint of relief valves
To prevent the stem from rising
checks.x: Always open valves slowly to minimize system pressure transients.

checks.q: What is the effect of opening a valve on flow and upstream backpressure?
o: Flow increases and upstream backpressure decreases
Flow decreases and upstream backpressure increases
checks.x: Opening a valve results in increased flow and decreased backpressure as measured upstream of the valve.

examples.title: Safety valve blowdown
examples.problem: A safety valve lifts at 200 psig and reseats at 190 psig. Find the blowdown as a percentage of the actuating pressure.
steps: Blowdown is the difference between setpoint and reset pressure: 200 - 190 = 10 psig.
Express it as a percentage of the setpoint: 10 / 200 x 100.

examples.title: Relief valve setpoint
examples.page: Word: Valve Fundamentals.docx, slide 1.88 Valve Setpoint Calculation
examples.problem: A spring holds a relief valve disk shut with 1000 lbf, and system pressure acts on 4 in² of disk area. At what pressure does the valve lift?
steps: The setpoint depends on spring force and the disk area on which pressure acts, so use P = F / A.
examples.cite: Word: Valve Fundamentals.docx, slide 1.88 Valve Setpoint Calculation

facts.q: What are the seven basic valve parts in objective 1.3 of ME-04?
facts.a: Body, bonnet, stem, actuator, packing, seat, and disk.

facts.q: What is the primary pressure boundary of a valve?
facts.a: The body, sometimes called the shell.

facts.q: What does a globe valve backseat do?
facts.a: It prevents system pressure from building against the valve packing.

facts.q: What is the main drawback of a globe valve?
facts.a: High head loss from two or more right angle turns of the fluid.

facts.q: What is a needle valve used for?
facts.a: Relatively fine adjustments in the amount of fluid flow.

facts.q: What does a reducing valve do?
facts.a: It automatically reduces supply pressure to a preselected pressure.

facts.q: What is the difference between direct-acting and reverse-acting pneumatic actuators?
facts.a: Direct-acting: air closes the valve and the spring opens it. Reverse-acting: air opens the valve and the spring closes it.

facts.q: How does a motor-operated valve fail on loss of power?

summary.text: A valve's basic parts are the body, bonnet, trim, actuator, and packing. Stem leakage is controlled by properly compressing the packing.
Gate valves give low resistance but do not throttle. Globe valves throttle well but have high head loss.
Ball valves give quarter turn on-off service, plug valves direct flow between ports, and diaphragm and pinch valves isolate the mechanism from the fluid.
Check valves prevent reverse flow, and safety and relief valves provide automatic overpressure protection.
Actuators are manual, electric motor, pneumatic, hydraulic, and solenoid.

blend_notes.note: The handbook p.38 says some lift check valves may be installed horizontally, with a ball held by guide ribs. Valve Fundamentals.docx slide 1.35 says vertically. The p.37 and slide 1.34 installation limits also differ. Neither detail is shown.

Slides 1.23 and 1.26 say ball and plug valves start, stop, or throttle. The handbook p.18 and p.21 say they stop or start, and p.19 and p.22 say they throttle poorly apart from special designs. The lesson uses the handbook.

The handbook p.35 lists swing, tilting-disk, piston, butterfly, and stop as the general check valve types and then teaches lift checks too. Slide 1.32 lists swing, lift, and stop. The lesson teaches swing, lift, and stop, which the objective names need. No values differ.

Flexible wedge steam service (p.11), steam service globe installation (p.18), composition disks for steam and hot water (p.17), hydraulic lock (slide 1.58), and water injection speed (p.49) are water-system material, so they are left off.
